item.title: Contrastive Astromer: Two-Stage Contrastive Representation Learning for Astronomical Light Curve Classification
item.description: arXiv:2611.00150v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large astronomical surveys collect abundant light curves, but reliable class labels remain scarce. ASTROMER 2 learns from unlabeled light curves by reconstructing masked observations, yet this objective does not explicitly encourage class separation in a compact representation of each light curve. We introduce Contrastive Astromer, a two-stage approach that makes these representations more useful for classification without changing the ASTROMER 2 encoder architecture. First, unsupervised contrastive learning on single-band MACHO light curves brings together representations of augmented views of the same object. Supervised contrastive learning, supported by an auxiliary classification loss, then uses a separate labeled Alcock sample to strengthen class discrimination. We evaluate the resulting representations by freezing the encoder and training a separate classifier. On a held-out set of 600 objects, this classifier achieves a macro-F1 of 0.7943 with 500 labeled examples per class, exceeding our reproduction of the ASTROMER 2 finetune-and-classify pipeline by 5.10 percentage points. With downstream classifier training budgets of 20 and 100 examples per class, macro-F1 reaches 0.7078 and 0.7704, respectively, also surpassing this baseline. Embedding-space analyses further show that supervised adaptation improves local class consistency and global class separation. These results show that contrastive adaptation makes pretrained light-curve representations more effective for classification and more informative about the structure of variability classes.
item.dc:creator: Justin Minggan Wei, Pavlos Protopapas, Guillermo Cabrera-Vives

item.title: Wide-field search for submicrosecond optical and gamma transients as manifestation of primordial black holes evaporation with the TAIGA-HiSCORE Cherenkov array
item.description: arXiv:2611.00160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrated in our papers [Panov, 2021; Panov,2025), that the TAIGA-HiSCORE Cherenkov array physics, originally designed for research in cosmic rays and ultra-high-energy gamma-ray astronomy, can also be used for wide-field searches for very rare submicrosecond optical transients of astrophysical origin. The papers \cite{PANOV-2021,PANOV-2025} presented the results of the first four seasons of optical transient searches (2018--2022) and the resulting upper limits on the flux of corresponding events. The present paper presents data processing from two new seasons of optical transient searches (2022--2024). This paper further develops a method for searching for narrow spatiotemporal groups of ultra-high-energy gamma-rays (above 100\,TeV). Since the evaporation of relic black holes can be accompanied by both by the emission of a short light pulse and by a flash of ultra-high-energy gamma-rays, a multimessenger technique for searching for black hole evaporation was in fact implemented in this work, where two different methods are implemented within a single instrument. The search for narrow spatiotemporal groups of gamma-rays was carried out in time windows of 1000\,$\mu$s, 100\,$\mu$s, and 6\,$\mu$s. Since narrow groups of gamma were not detected, the upper limit on their frequency were obtained as $10^{-3}\,\mathrm{ster}^{-1}\mathrm{h}^{-1}$. The upper limit on the number of submicrosecond optical transients have also been updated: $10^{-4}\mathrm{erg/s/cm}^2$ as $5\cdot10^{-4}\,\mathrm{ster}^{-1}\mathrm{h}^{-1}$.

item.title: Shear Mapping in Python (SMPy): Modular, Extensible, and Accessible Dark Matter Mapping
item.description: arXiv:2611.00225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the Universe's large-scale distribution of dark matter is a central objective in the era of precision cosmology. A key technique for the study of dark matter is weak gravitational lensing: a phenomenon where light from distant galaxies is sheared as it passes through the gravitational field of a massive object, like a galaxy cluster. This shear, which manifests as a slight (weak) distortion of shapes over thousands of galaxies, allows astrophysicists to infer the distribution of total matter, including both luminous and dark matter. Obtaining a mass distribution from a catalog of galaxy shears involves reconstructing the convergence ($\kappa$), the projected surface mass density divided by the critical surface density for the lens-source system. The Shear Mapping in Python (SMPy) package provides a standardized, well-documented, and open-source solution for creating convergence maps from weak lensing galaxy shear measurements. SMPy implements three mapping methods: the classic Kaiser-Squires inversion, aperture mass mapping, and, to our knowledge, the first publicly available implementation of the full KS+ algorithm, which corrects for missing data, field borders, and reduced shear. SMPy was initially developed to support the Superpressure Balloon-borne Imaging Telescope (SuperBIT) and has since evolved into a general-purpose tool suitable for analyzing the weak lensing data from cosmological surveys.
item.dc:creator: Georgios N. Vassilakis, Jacqueline E. McCleary, Maya Amit, Sayan Saha

item.title: Detection and excision of radio-frequency interference in radio arrays
item.description: arXiv:2611.01308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The detection and excision of radio-frequency interference (RFI) is usually approached by asking how best to identify RFI within a given data product. I address a prior question: which data product is a given RFI emitter is most detectable in? I develop a model for the suppression of RFI in visibilities and tied-array beams by the antenna primary beam, near-field wavefront curvature, bandwidth smearing, and fringe tracking. The comparison between antenna-based and array-based detection reduces to a single quantity related to the mean per-baseline RFI coherence. Cross-correlation detection is preferred only above a coherence threshold of $(N-1)^{-1/2}$, where $N$ is the number of antennas. I evaluate this model for four array configurations (the Very Large Array A and D configurations, and the fixed MeerKAT and Deep Synoptic Array / DSA configurations) and five representative RFI emitters spanning distances of 5\,km to medium-Earth orbit. Compact, filled, arrays favor the cross-correlations for stationary terrestrial emitters, whereas extended sparse arrays do not. RFI emitters with significant motion relative to radio arrays, in particular aircraft and low- and medium-Earth-orbit satellites, favor the sum of antenna autocorrelations everywhere by one to seven orders of magnitude, because their coherence is destroyed by rapid fringe rotation. For RFI below the single-antenna noise, no phase-unknown cross-correlation statistic is more sensitive than the autocorrelation sum. Tied-array beams are the least sensitive data product of all: the array factor supplies no suppression of terrestrial RFI, so a beam sees an emitter as a single antenna does. I describe a real-time, GPU-based implementation of autocorrelation-based excision for the 110-antenna Deep Synoptic Array, and outline the design implications for upcoming arrays.
item.dc:creator: Vikram Ravi

item.title: FiDeR: Denoising Astronomical Images at the Observational Resolution
item.description: arXiv:2611.01657v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Finite-iteration Deconvolution--Reconvolution Denoising (FiDeR), a method for reducing noise in astronomical images while retaining approximately the input point-spread function (PSF). We first apply a finite number of Richardson--Lucy (RL) iterations to the nonnegative source-plus-background image. We then measure the response of a calibration point source processed with the same settings and derive a reconvolution kernel matched to the observational PSF. The calibration includes the background-to-source flux ratio. We compare FiDeR with six denoisers using simulated point-source and mixed stellar--galaxy fields, and observations from the James Webb Space Telescope Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) and Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI). In the stellar tests, bright-source widths remain close to the input widths; faint sources show small residual offsets. For the mixed field, FiDeR reaches peak signal-to-noise ratios of 46.701 and 44.850 dB at backgrounds of 10 and 20 counts per pixel, with wing errors of 0.657 and 0.858 counts. It also gives small aperture-flux and shape errors, although block-matching and three-dimensional filtering (BM3D) gives higher structural similarity. The NIRCam data show lower core and combined-region errors, while the three-exposure MIRI test gives benefits mainly in the stellar aperture and photometry. These results support substantial noise reduction with little change in the measured PSF within the tested regimes. The denoised images can provide inputs for further reconstruction and measurement; their uncertainties must account for residual noise correlations.
item.dc:creator: Lei Wang, Bin Li, Lin Nie, Zhaojun Yan, Xuechun Chen, Yachong Diao, Huanyuan Shan

item.title: Aperture Photometric Accuracy of Point-spread-function-deconvolved Astronomical Images
item.description: arXiv:2611.01670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces an improved Richardson--Lucy (RL) framework utilizing negative backfilling (NB) and the novel filtered image deconvolution and noise backfilling (FiDNoBa) algorithm. By integrating a low-pass prefiltering stage---specifically employing a Kalman filter---with the reintegration of filtered-out noise components after RL iterations, we effectively suppress noise artifacts while maintaining rigorous flux integrity. We extensively evaluate our Kalman + RL + NB approach using both numerical simulations and real observational data. Simulations across three regimes demonstrate superior photometric accuracy, reducing the relative mean deviation (RMD) to below 1\% for isolated sources, maintaining high fidelity (RMD $\sim$0.37\%) for blended S\'{e}rsic galaxies, and achieving $\sim$5\% RMD in crowded stellar fields while significantly increasing source recovery rates compared to traditional point-spread function photometry. Crucially, we validate the practical efficacy of FiDNoBa on real space-based (JWST/NIRCam) and ground-based (Very Large Telescope Survey Telescope OmegaCAM) images. The results confirm that our method reliably handles complex instrumental signatures, such as the extended wings of the STPSF, mitigating the severe ringing artifacts typical of traditional RL deconvolution while ensuring highly stable aperture photometry in practical survey processing.
item.dc:creator: Shen Zhang, Lei Wang, Yachong Diao, Zhaojun Yan, Xiyan Peng, Yao Liu, Huanyuan Shan, Guanghuan Wang, Fengshan Liu, Chengliang Wei, Lin Nie, Xuechun Chen, Hengkai Ding, Zhenya Zheng

item.title: From Rock Tumbling to Telescope Mirror Grinding: How Optical Perfection Emerges from Random Motion
item.description: arXiv:2611.01673v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When two glass disks are rubbed together by hand with an abrasive between them, their surfaces spontaneously converge to perfectly matching spherical curves, accurate to tens of nanometers. How does such optical precision emerge from an essentially random manual process? Starting from Preston's law of material removal, we derive a first-principles explanation. Symmetries of the grinding stroke imply that planes and spheres are the generic equilibria of the process. Their stability is governed by a hierarchy of timescales: small-scale irregularities decay exponentially on the grinding timescale $T_\text{grind}$, while large-scale deviations from a sphere diffuse away on the longer spherizing timescale $T_\text{sphere} \propto (R_\text{mirror}/R_\text{stroke})^2\, T_\text{grind}$. Gravity and finite disk size destabilize planar surfaces, but for sufficiently short strokes spheres remain stable ($T_\text{deform} \gg T_\text{sphere}$), with only their radius of curvature varying adiabatically. The same framework unifies telescope mirror grinding with everyday phenomena: rock tumbling (explaining why rotary tumbling rounds edges more than vibratory, and why neither produce spheres) and sanding (explaining why small flat surfaces inevitably round). These examples offer an accessible classroom context for stable and unstable equilibria, exponential relaxation, diffusion, multi-timescale analysis, and the emergence of the Laplacian operator from averaging over a local area.
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Schaan

item.title: Deconvolved IXPE Polarization Maps of the Crab Nebula in a Maximum-a-Posteriori Framework
item.description: arXiv:2611.01820v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze the first IXPE observation of the Crab Nebula using a polarization-resolved deconvolution method based on maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation. The method reconstructs the polarization-resolved intensity map as a three-dimensional distribution in sky-position and polarization-angle spaces, using an instrumental response that depends on the incident direction and polarization angle of X-ray photons. We apply the method to the IXPE data in the 2-8~keV band and compare the result with that obtained using the basic analysis. Our result shows sharper spatial structure, making the jet shape more clearly identifiable than that in the basic analysis. The reconstructed image shows a statistically significant tendency for the magnetic-field orientation to be perpendicular to the intensity-gradient orientation in the jet region. Although these results are obtained by using a simplified response where systematic uncertainty remains, they demonstrate that our MAP-based deconvolution can improve the interpretability of IXPE polarization maps for nebular sources.
item.dc:creator: Keisuke Uchiyama, Mikio Morii, Toru Tamagawa

item.title: The Agentic Observer Hackathon: Autonomous Decision-making in Simulated Astronomical Surveys
item.description: arXiv:2611.01988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Astronomical surveys must allocate observing time while responding to changing conditions and competing scientific priorities. We present the Agentic Observer Hackathon (AOH), a community challenge for studying autonomous survey operations. Within a synthetic multi-object survey with prescribed exposure responses and assignment constraints, decision systems select pointings, assign targets and choose exposure configurations while responding to observing requests, instrumental faults and data loss. We evaluate systems submitted by 102 teams on campaigns reserved for evaluation and analyse target completion in a reference campaign. The leading systems combine numerical exposure planning with language models for interpreting operational information and supporting longer-term decisions. Exploratory tests show improved fault reporting with model access in several systems, while revised scientific priorities produce substantial changes in ranking. The reference campaign traces target completion and diagnoses errors in the baseline's inference of prescribed quality bands. The released simulator and reference strategies provide common survey conditions for comparing exposure allocation, target selection and recovery from interruptions.
item.dc:creator: Haosong Wang, Ting Tan, Yao Li, Huanyuan Shan, Dezi Liu, Xiangkun Liu, Yifei Luo, Wei Wang, Zonghuan Wu, Zhongxu Zhai

item.title: The Transient Array Radio Telescope: An open-source all-sky imaging radio interferometer
item.description: arXiv:2611.02313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Transient Array Radio Telescope (TART) is an open-source 24-element 1573-1577 MHz L-band imaging interferometer designed for research and education. This paper introduces the physical architecture of the TART, describes it's electronics, radios, correlator, and the design of the antenna array. Then we discuss the software architecture, including the calibration of the telescope using satellites and imaging pipelines. Imaging results are presented, which lead to an estimate of ~52 kJy for the sensitivity of the telescope.
item.dc:creator: Timothy C. A. Molteno, Max Scheel, Pat Suggate, Ben V. Hugo, Phil Brown

item.title: Characterisation Methodology for Persistence and Anti-persistence in IR Detectors for the Euclid and SVOM Space Missions
item.description: arXiv:2611.02860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: H2RG and ALFA are the infrared detectors used in the Euclid and SVOM space missions. These types of detectors may be affected by persistence and anti-persistence, phenomena that distort pixel responses after exposure to light due to simultaneous trapping and release of charges within the pixel. These phenomena have shown to cause biases in flux measurements and potentially false detections, among other effects. This article presents a universal methodology for characterising persistence and anti-persistence using differential ramps, Savitzky--Golay filtering, and non-linearity correction. When applied to ground characterisation data, this approach reveals spatial inhomogeneities, environmental dependencies (in particular fluence, flux, temperature and wavelength), and unexpected spectral effects in ALFA. These preliminary results validate the method and pave the way for in-flight correction models capable of meeting the missions' accuracy requirements.
item.dc:creator: Naomie De Araujo, Aur\'elia Secroun, Marie Tourneur Silvain, \'Eric Kajfasz, Eliott Robineau, Alioune Diop

item.title: Anomaly-ranked confirmation slows new-class learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.03250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anomaly detectors rank unfamiliar examples for expert confirmation, and the confirmed examples teach a classifier to recognise a new class. Across five benchmarks from physics, medicine and computer vision, the members flagged by the detector are those the classifier learns first. In three systems, confirming the highest-ranked members of a new class gives lower recognition than confirming the same number of random members. Handing subsequent selection to the promoted classifier recovers part of this loss in two systems. A paired intervention further shows that replacing nearby known classes with distant ones sharply reduces the confirmations needed for recognition. These results distinguish finding a new class from selecting examples that teach its extent: within the tested classes, concentrating confirmations at the top of the anomaly ranking makes learning less efficient.
item.dc:creator: Argyro Sasli, Michael Coughlin

item.title: Detectability of an orbital-angular-momentum-based gravitational wave detector
item.description: arXiv:2611.00085v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The orbital angular momentum (OAM) of light provides a new approach to probing gravitational waves (GWs) through transitions between OAM states. Here, we assess the detectability of an OAM-based GW detector by developing a readout scheme and evaluating its noise budget over the frequency range from $1~\mathrm{mHz}$ to $100~\mathrm{Hz}$, including laser-intensity noise, laser-phase noise, mode-impurity noise, and shot noise. For a symmetric superposition OAM state, the GW-induced transition amplitudes satisfy $\alpha_+=-\alpha_-^*$, whereas the noise-induced mode-crosstalk coefficients obey $n_+=n_-^*$. Hence, the GW-induced signal forms a differential-mode contribution, while laser-intensity and mode-impurity noises enter as common-mode contributions, enabling their suppression by the balanced detection. Under a fixed beam-waist constraint, a shorter arm permits a larger paraxial parameter, reducing the equivalent angular-noise strain sensitivity. We adopt an arm length of $L=4\,\mathrm{m}$, $N=160$ round trips, a paraxial parameter of $\gamma=0.1$, a laser power incident on the beam splitter of $P_{\mathrm{BS}}=10\,\mathrm{kW}$, and a wavelength of $\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}=1064\,\mathrm{nm}$. Using representative noise spectra, we find that, for GWs from an equal-mass binary black hole with source-frame component masses of $M_{\mathrm{src}}=10^{4}\,M_{\odot}$ at redshift $z=1$, balanced detection yields an SNR of $24.7$ for an imbalance parameter of $\epsilon=10^{-3}$ and $239$ for $\epsilon=10^{-5}$, with the sensitivity approaching the shot-noise limit in the latter case. These results highlight the importance of a compact optical configuration and strong common-mode rejection for realizing an OAM-based GW detector.
item.dc:creator: Haorong Wu, Xilong Fan

item.title: First-principles calculations of far-wing absorption in He-broadened CO2 infrared spectra
item.description: arXiv:2611.00188v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We report theoretical predictions and modeling of the far-wing absorption of CO2 broadened by He over a wide temperature range (200-1000 K), which are relevant for exoplanet atmosphere studies. Accurate modeling of He-broadened CO2 absorption is essential for opacity calculations used to characterize the composition, structure, and climate of exoplanet atmospheres. In particular, the strong CO2 band at 4.3 mum has been clearly identified in the spectra of several exoplanets observed with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). Requantized classical molecular dynamics simulations were first performed to predict absorption in the far wings of the 4.3 mum band of CO2. The resulting predictions show excellent agreement with available experimental data at room temperature. The theoretical predictions and measured data were then used to parameterize an impact energy-corrected sudden model, which allowed us to accurately reproduce the far-wing absorption of He-broadened CO2 in several infrared spectral regions over the (200-1000) K temperature range. Finally, for applications to exoplanet atmosphere opacity calculations, we derived temperature-dependent chi-factor corrections that account for the sub-Lorentzian behavior of the far wing of the major infrared bands of CO2.
item.dc:creator: Ha Tran, Emile Ducreux

item.title: CHIME All-sky Multiday Pulsar Stacking Search (CHAMPSS): Power Spectrum Injections and Survey Sensitivity
item.description: arXiv:2611.00341v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial signal injection into real data is a key tool in time-domain radio astronomy, with particular import to the study of pulsars and Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs). Many surveys inject into the time series to probe observational biases impacting the detection of radio transients. In the case of the CHIME All-sky Multiday Pulsar Stack Search (CHAMPSS), the computational demands of both hardware and software time series injections force an alternative approach. We present methods for injecting artificial pulsar signals into the Fourier power spectrum. The injection process detailed here is computationally negligible compared to the overhead of the CHAMPSS search pipeline. We use injections to probe the in-system biases of the CHAMPSS survey. CHAMPSS is most sensitive to pulsars with frequencies on the order of 0.1 - 100 Hz and fluxes > 1 mJy. Our injections show weak overall sensitivity dependence on other factors such as dispersion measure (DM), duty cycle, and sky coordinates, but complex non-monotonic interactions between all parameters. Our findings suggest that frequency-dependent noise, especially low-frequency or "red" noise, and sampling limitations at higher frequencies are the dominant extrinsic factors decreasing CHAMPSS' sensitivity to pulsars.
item.dc:creator: Reynier Squillace, Lars K\"unkel, Robert Main, Scott M. Ransom, Wenke Xia, Kathryn Crowter, Victoria Kaspi, Ingrid Stairs, Hudson Bridgwater, Bradley Meyers, Alexander Saffer

item.title: Nonlinear Physics and Self-Organized Criticality in Astrophysics
item.description: arXiv:2611.01119v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The definition of self-organized criticality (SOC) is ambiguous and controversial. Here we discuss the nonlinear physics of six basic SOC definitions, such as: phase transitions, fractal structures, power laws, SOC contingency, exponential growth, and diffusive decay. Statistics of SOC events or avalanche processes can be inferred from their size distributions, or from their spatio-temporal evolution.
item.dc:creator: Markus J. Aschwanden

item.title: Mean-element Parareal: Parallel-in-Time Integration of the Solar System
item.description: arXiv:2611.01237v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-term integrations of planetary systems have long been considered inherently sequential: each time step must start from the exact state at the end of the previous one, because any error in that state, however small, is amplified by orbital shear and chaos and alters the trajectory. Because a single step of a modern Wisdom--Holman integrator takes only ~100 ns - too short to split across cores - additional cores have previously only been used to run multiple simulations in parallel. We introduce mean-element parareal (MEP), a parallel-in-time scheme that accelerates a single Solar System integration (eight planets, general relativity) at the same accuracy as the serial integrator. Combined with a latency-optimized C kernel that integrates 5 Gyr on one core in 5.8 h, MEP completes a 5 Gyr integration in 52 min on 64 cores (a parallel speed-up of 6.7x, and 10.4x faster than the previous 9.0 h single-core record) or in 1.8 h on 16 cores (3.3x parallel speed-up, 5.0x faster than the previous record). MEP succeeds because its coarse propagator uses a numerical first-order mean-element theory to remove the short-period oscillations from the semi-major axes, preventing Keplerian shear from amplifying them into growing phase errors. Standard parareal with a coarse Wisdom-Holman integrator fails for planetary orbits because no inexpensive coarse integrator can resolve these oscillations. To our knowledge, this is the first measured multicore speed-up of a single long-term planetary integration and opens a pathway towards larger-scale parallelization.
item.dc:creator: Michael Hippke

item.title: Learned Surrogates of Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence
item.description: arXiv:2611.01356v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, the flow of astrophysical and fusion plasmas, is costly to simulate. We present, to our knowledge, the first learned surrogates of three-dimensional resistive MHD turbulence, and compare three standard backbones in that role: a convolutional UNet, a shifted-window transformer and a Fourier neural operator. They are trained as autoregressive emulators of decaying MHD turbulence at a resolution of $128^3$ and Reynolds numbers of 1000, 3000 and 6000, on 500 simulations per Reynolds number, each with one two-stage procedure, single steps and then short rollouts, and stopped by one rule. Over a window of about one large-eddy turnover time, the UNet and the transformer reach relative velocity errors of 0.018 to 0.053 and keep the current sheets, the enstrophy, the current density and the energy spectra of the simulation; which of the two is the more accurate depends on the Reynolds number, the UNet leading at 3000 and 6000 and the transformer at 1000. Applied with the same backbones and training procedure to two public benchmarks, the models reach the lowest error reported to date on the isotropic turbulence set of FactFormer, 39% below the best published model. On the compressible MHD set of The Well, their rollout errors are a third to a half below those of the best of The Well's baselines. They also match a 1.3 B-parameter pretrained foundation model in its rollout windows, with 20-62 times fewer parameters. The code, the configuration of every model, the evaluation scripts and the data generator with the seed of every simulation will be released upon publication.
item.dc:creator: Semih Kacmaz, E. A. Huerta

item.title: Choosing a generator for streaming Gaussian noise in gravitational-wave mock data: accuracy, cost and reproducibility
item.description: arXiv:2611.01624v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mock data challenges need long stretches of colored Gaussian noise with a prescribed spectrum. The candidates are the crossfade of independently drawn windows that the standard gravitational-wave libraries implement, overlap-save finite-impulse-response filtering, autoregressive and autoregressive moving-average (ARMA) models, and the reproducible filter of PyCBC. One measure ranks them all: the covariance error against the target over the analysis band, evaluated from each generator's algebra; generated noise only checks the implementations. We also measure throughput, retained state and the cost of bit-exact regeneration. With the target continued smoothly below the band, the crossfade with windows of 256 s or more reaches an error below $10^{-3}$ on all eleven detector curves as tabulated, at about 4.7 million samples per second from a state of a few hundred bytes. An overlap-save filter is faster but needs tens of thousands of taps for an error of a few percent, and no tested autoregressive or ARMA configuration lies on the accuracy--throughput fronts. An error of $10^{-3}$ needs a window of 8 to 235 s, longest on the design curves with narrow lines, where it also depends on the tabulation. With the target cut at the band edge, as current generators do by default, every method has an error above one half on the projected Advanced LIGO (aLIGO) O4 curve, and the crossfade on five other curves. The crossfade is cyclostationary. With the continued target, its cyclic part is the larger part of the error only at 8 s, on the aLIGO O4 and the Virgo and KAGRA design curves, and stays within a factor of two of the stationary part on the aLIGO O3 and the Virgo and KAGRA design curves. We recommend the crossfade with a window from the table of detector curves, and a smooth continuation of the target below the band.
item.dc:creator: Isaac C. F. Wong

item.title: Simulating winds in the Galactic centre. II. Observational biases on HI clouds and a multi-wavelength comparison
item.description: arXiv:2611.02144v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-velocity neutral hydrogen (HI) clouds found up to several kiloparsecs above the Galactic centre (GC) provide some of the most direct evidence for a nuclear wind in the Milky Way, yet the properties inferred for these clouds are influenced by how they are observed. Starting from a magnetohydrodynamical simulation in which supernova feedback drives a multiphase nuclear outflow, we generate mock HI observations matched to the angular resolution and sensitivity of Green Bank Telescope (GBT) surveys of the GC and analyse them in the same way as the real data. We find that observational effects substantially reshape the cloud population: beam smearing makes clouds appear larger, rounder and more diffuse, while noise erases faint clouds and strips low-density gas from the others. These effects combined, together with confusion with foreground disk emission, prevent the detection of more than 80% of the clouds (up to 95% during more quiescent phases), while those detected appear less massive, less turbulent and less elongated, with column densities underestimated by a factor of two; only their velocities are reliably recovered. Once these effects are included, the simulated clouds broadly reproduce the properties and sky distribution of the GBT population, but lack the fastest (> 250 km/s ) and highest-latitude (b > 10{\deg} ) clouds. Mock UV absorption and soft X-ray observations support this picture, with warm-ionized gas column densities at the low end of the observed range and X-ray emission measures too low at b > 10{\deg} . Our results imply that the true GC cloud population is more numerous, massive, turbulent and elongated than observed, and that fully reproducing observations may require a stronger recent starburst or additional feedback.
item.dc:creator: N. Peschken, E. M. Di Teodoro, M. Hanasz, L. Armillotta, D. Woltanski, A. Gawryszczak

item.title: Solving the Mystery of the Electron Radiation Belt at Uranus: Leveraging Knowledge of Earth's Radiation Belts in a Re-Examination of Voyager 2 Observations
item.description: arXiv:2611.02221v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Voyager 2 provided the only direct measurement of the radiation environment at Uranus and established the well-accepted characterization of a system with a weaker ion radiation belt and surprisingly intense electron radiation belt. Recent re-analysis of the flyby, however, suggests that these observations were not taken during normal solar wind conditions, and instead occurred while a large solar wind transient, a corotating interaction region, was passing over the system. With this context, this study compares the Voyager 2 observations to a similar event observed at Earth. This comparative approach, along with an expanded contextual interpretation of the Voyager 2 flyby, suggests that solar wind-magnetospheric interactions at Uranus may have driven enhanced lower band chorus wave emissions capable of accelerating electrons to relativistic energies. This motivates new, more expansive questions to be explored at Uranus and highlights the need for a Uranus orbiter mission.
item.dc:creator: R. C. Allen, S. K. Vines, G. C. Ho

item.title: Harmonic Angular Mapping Method for Binary Microlensing Grid Search
item.description: arXiv:2611.02326v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Searching for binary-lens microlensing solutions is computationally demanding because of the complex parameter space and the large number of trial models required. We present an algorithm that accelerates binary-lens grid searches by expanding the angular dependence of precomputed magnification maps in Fourier modes. By contracting the observation-dependent weighted sums in Fourier space, the $\chi^2$ values for all trial source-trajectory angles can be evaluated efficiently using inverse fast Fourier transforms (FFTs), avoiding repeated calculations over individual observations. We tested the method on 200 Roman-like synthetic binary-lens events. For 166 events (83%), the recovered fits agreed with Levenberg--Marquardt fits initialized at the injected parameters to within $|\Delta\chi^2|\leq1$. The FFT map scan required an average of 5.05~min per event. For the same discrete search volume, the Fourier angular evaluation was estimated to be approximately 900 times faster than conventional magnification-map sampling. These results demonstrate that the method can efficiently identify useful initial conditions for binary-lens light-curve modeling.
item.dc:creator: Kansuke Nunota

item.title: Imaging the Current Distribution in Superconducting Transition-Edge Sensors with Scanning SQUID Microscopy
item.description: arXiv:2611.02352v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transition-edge sensors (TESs) exploit the resistive transition of a superconductor to detect minute changes in temperature. While significant progress has been made in understanding the temperature- and current-dependent resistive transition in these devices, important aspects of TES behavior under bias remain unresolved. In particular, existing TES models largely neglect spatial variations in the superconducting state and current distribution arising from device geometry and proximity effects associated with the superconducting leads and normal metal features. Using scanning superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) microscopy (SSM), we directly image local superconducting properties and transport current in two molybdenum-gold (MoAu) X-ray TES designs. We measure the local diamagnetic response to identify superconducting regions in devices voltage-biased within the transition and the Oersted field generated by the transport current to reconstruct the corresponding current distribution. We observe bias-dependent reconfigurations of the current distribution that track current-induced changes in superconducting regions, highlighting the importance of mesoscale spatial variations for TES device physics, operation, and design.
item.dc:creator: Samantha Walker, Austin Kaczmarek, Douglas A. Bennett, Jason E. Austermann, W. Bertrand Doriese, Shannon M. Duff, Johannes Hubmayr, Kelsey M. Morgan, Daniel R. Schmidt, Daniel S. Swetz, Joel N. Ullom, Joel Weber, Michael D. Niemack, Katja C. Nowack

item.title: A Century-Long Archival Search and Analysis of the Rubin Observatory-Discovered Dwarf Planet Candidate 2026 ED$_{138}$
item.description: arXiv:2611.02371v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The trans-Neptunian object (TNO) 2026 ED$_{138}$ was discovered in early data from the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, and recovered in Dark Energy Camera images back to 2016. With an absolute magnitude of $H_V = 3.11 \pm 0.05$ mag, it is one of the largest known TNOs, with a diameter of 635-1590 km for geometric albedos between 0.25 and 0.04. Its position far to the south and close to the galactic plane kept it hidden in images that recorded it for decades. Here, we present archival observations of 2026 ED$_{138}$ spanning 89 years: twelve photographic plates taken between 1954 and 2000, a marginal detection on a 1937 Harvard plate, 2010-2017 VISTA near-infrared images, 2016-2020 SkyMapper images, and ten years of ATLAS photometry. The archival positions improve the long-term ephemeris fivefold, and we predict 15 occultations of $G \leq 16.5$ mag stars in 2027-2030, six of which will occur over populated land. The line of sight from Earth has turned by $\sim87^\circ$ since 1954, yet the plate magnitudes remain consistent with the present-day phase curve. Fitted plate by plate, they exclude oblate shapes with $c/a \leq 0.6$ for at least half of all spin-axis orientations and, with a present-day light curve amplitude below $\sim0.11-0.15$ mag, a Haumea-like Jacobi ellipsoid for $\sim90\%$ of them. We find a tentative 10.4 h light curve period ($\sim20.7$ h if double-peaked). Near-infrared colors place 2026 ED$_{138}$ in the BR (intermediate red) taxonomic class, with $J-H = 0.60\pm0.15$, redder than Haumea and without evidence of similar 1.5 $\mu$m water-ice absorption, supporting the conclusion that it is not a Haumea-family member. $z$-band photometry also limits Eris-like methane to $\lesssim25\%$ of the surface. Integrations over $\pm1$ Gyr show it sticks to the 12:7 resonance with Neptune for tens of megayears at a time, but it rarely remains permanently captured.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Murtagh, Colin Orion Chandler, Mario Juri\'c, Ian Chow, Pedro H. Bernardinelli, Bruno M. Perroni, Ryder Strauss, Sam Deen, Hugues Talbot, Matthew J. Holman, Kevin J. Napier

item.title: Are habitable-zone TESS Objects of Interest really there? Period resolution from the full archive
item.description: arXiv:2611.03019v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: TESS Objects of Interest (TOIs) seen as single or duo transits carry a catalogue period that is undefined or equal to the separation of the two events, and their insolation and any habitable-zone label inherit it. We reanalyse all 187 TOIs catalogued with P = 0 or P >= 200 d using all public TESS data through Sector 107, with a flux-based method that weights each alias by per-epoch transit likelihoods, the transit duration and a geometric prior, and tests for coherence, data edges, contamination by other planets and instrumental artefacts. It recovers 12 published periods blindly and, in injection-recovery tests, 71 per cent of periods constrained by a new transit, with no wrong period. It resolves 28 periods and fixes 8 more by exclusion. Are habitable-zone TOIs really there? Mostly not: of the 28 duo-transits that a catalogue-period criterion places in the conservative habitable zone, about two are expected to lie there, both giants, and none of the 12 planet-sized ones; those resolved are aliases of hotter planets. Conversely, habitable-zone planets hide behind missing or wrong periods: we recover three published M-dwarf examples and validate four planets with new periods, including TOI-2298 b, a 3.0 Earth-radius sub-Neptune at 146.58 d in the conservative habitable zone of a K dwarf, and TOI-6075 b, a 1.7 Earth-radius planet at 416.5 d (833 d not excluded), the second validated transiting planet smaller than 2 Earth radii with P > 1 yr. We release alias-marginalised habitable-zone probabilities for the whole sample.
item.dc:creator: Juan F. Pag\'es Navarrete

item.title: Statistical Modeling of Foreground Galactic Cirrus for Diffuse Halo Light Measurement
item.description: arXiv:2611.03172v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Galactic cirrus, the diffuse Milky Way starlight scattered by interstellar dust, has become a major source of systematic uncertainty in measurements of extragalactic diffuse emission at ultra-low surface brightness levels. Proper modeling and correction of this foreground is crucial to unlock the full potential of next-generation deep imaging surveys for studies of faint diffuse emission such as galactic stellar halos, ultra-diffuse galaxies, and intracluster light (ICL). We develop a statistical approach to reconstruct the 2D distribution of the Galactic cirrus while preserving the underlying diffuse extragalactic emission from stellar halos. We combine the broad dust morphology traced by far-infrared emission with multiscale structural information extracted from the optical images. The method synthesizes plausible cirrus structures through iteratively refining the foreground, the smooth diffuse light model, and the residual sky. The performance is assessed through injection--recovery experiments using Euclid VIS observations of the Abell 2390 cluster, which show substantial improvements in recovered stellar halo photometry, although residual biases depend on the local foreground structure and sky estimation. We apply the method to the central Abell 2390 field to correct for a prominent cirrus complex near its brightest cluster galaxy (BCG), revealing a smoother BCG+ICL distribution with a steeper outer light profile and reduced contamination in the integrated light. Our results demonstrate the potential of statistical modeling of Galactic cirrus to improve diffuse light photometry in deep wide-field imaging surveys.
item.dc:creator: Qing Liu, Henk Hoekstra, Ama\"el Ellien

item.title: Statistical Machine Learning for Astronomy -- A Textbook
item.description: arXiv:2506.12230v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This textbook gives a systematic treatment of statistical machine learning for astronomical research, based on Bayesian inference. It shows how modern data analysis techniques connect to classical statistical methods and follow from familiar statistical principles. The Bayesian perspective, used throughout, gives priority to uncertainty quantification and statistical rigor, which scientific inference in astronomy needs. The textbook progresses from probability theory and Bayesian inference through supervised learning, including linear regression with measurement uncertainties, logistic regression and classification. Unsupervised learning topics cover Principal Component Analysis and clustering methods. We then introduce sampling and Markov Chain Monte Carlo, followed by Gaussian Processes as probabilistic nonparametric methods and neural networks in the broader statistical context. Our theory-focused approach derives each method from first principles with complete mathematical development and then shows its astronomical applications. We put statistical insight first and explain why algorithms work, when they are appropriate, and how they connect to broader statistical principles. From a solid grounding in classical methods and their theory, the treatment leads to modern techniques such as neural networks. With this grounding, readers can apply the methods to astronomical research with proper attention to assumptions, limits and uncertainty propagation, as large astronomical surveys require. The 22 companion tutorials apply the methods to astronomical data in Jupyter notebooks.
item.dc:creator: Yuan-Sen Ting

item.title: Pixellated Posterior Sampling of Point Spread Functions in Astronomical Images
item.description: arXiv:2511.19594v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a novel framework for upsampled Point Spread Function (PSF) modeling using pixel-level Bayesian inference. Accurate PSF characterization is critical for precision measurements in many fields including: weak lensing, astrometry, and photometry. Our method defines the posterior distribution of the pixelized PSF model through the combination of an analytic Gaussian likelihood and a highly expressive generative diffusion model prior, trained on a library of HST ePSF templates. Compared to traditional methods (parametric Moffat, ePSF template-based, and regularized likelihood), we demonstrate that our PSF models achieve orders of magnitude higher likelihood and residuals consistent with noise, all while remaining visually realistic. Further, the method applies even for faint and heavily masked point sources, merely producing a broader posterior. By recovering a realistic, pixel-level posterior distribution, our technique enables the first meaningful propagation of detailed PSF morphological uncertainty in downstream analysis. An implementation of our posterior sampling procedure is available on GitHub.
item.dc:creator: Connor Stone, Ronan Legin, Alexandre Adam, Esmeralda Whitammer, Gabriel Missael Barco, Laurence Perreaul-Levasseur, Yashar Hezaveh

item.title: LISA science ground segment conventions
item.description: arXiv:2603.22377v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This document sets out the conventions used for data simulations, waveforms, and analysis pipelines within the Distributed Data Processing Centre (DDPC) of the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). It can also be considered a best practice guide for all publications related to the LISA mission. Topics covered include time-to-frequency transformations, gravitational-wave source parametrization, the instrumental response to gravitational waves, time-delay interferometry, and reference frame definitions.
item.dc:creator: Quentin Baghi, Stanislas Babak, Leor Barack, Jean-Baptiste Bayle, Ollie Burke, Raffi Enficiaud, Hector Estelles, Cecilio Garc\'ia Quir\'os, Olaf Hartwig, Aurelien Hees, Sascha Husa, Henri Inchausp\'e, Eric Joffre, Antoine Klein, Philip Lynch, Sylvain Marsat, Jonathan Menu, Zach Nasipak, Ramon Pardo De Santayana, Harald Pfeiffer, Lorenzo Pompili, Adam Pound, Geraint Pratten, Antoni Ramos-Buades, Carlos Sopuerta, Niels Warburton

item.title: A dual-polarization whitened-template trigger for real-time radio detection of extensive air showers
item.description: arXiv:2608.19898v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Autonomous radio detection of extensive air showers requires reliable discrimination of their characteristic signals from transient interference, with decisions made in real time under stringent hardware constraints. We present a compact dual-polarization trigger developed using detector-folded air-shower simulations and measured radio backgrounds from the Auger Engineering Radio Array. The method combines the characteristic shape of air-shower pulses with measured background statistics to construct a filter that distinguishes air-shower signals from radio interference. On an independent validation dataset, it achieves 96% signal efficiency at a frame-equivalent background trigger rate of 3.12 kHz, substantially outperforming conventional amplitude thresholding and unwhitened template matching. Its robustness is further investigated using recordings acquired at different times from geographically distributed stations exposed to heterogeneous radio interference. Transferring the unchanged filter between these environments requires adjusting the trigger threshold to the recently measured background conditions to control the background trigger rate. With threshold updates every 1 ms, the achieved rates range from 35.2 to 41.4 kHz for a nominal target of 35.7 kHz, demonstrating effective rate control across the tested environments while maintaining sensitivity to air-shower signals. The compact trigger architecture meets the timing constraints of a field-programmable gate array at 200 MHz, supporting its feasibility for autonomous radio detection.
item.dc:creator: Qader Dorosti, Alperen Aksoy, Ilja Bekman, Markus Cristinziani, Eric-Teunis de Boone, Vesselin Dimitrov, Chimezie Eguzo, Stefan Heidbrink, Stefan van Waasen, Andre Zambanini

item.title: Modeling the technical specifications for future multi-object spectroscopy instrumentation
item.description: arXiv:2608.22172v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate a proof-of-concept code designed to model the functionality of current generation astronomical fiber positioner instruments. This code accommodates an arbitrary number of fiber probes and astronomical targets. To establish the prerequisites for future fiber positioning technologies, we conduct a systematic analysis of both the observational and instrumentation parameter space (such as target density, fiber density, and exclusion and patrol radius). The tool assesses the efficiency and completeness of such a system by modeling the allocation of fibers to targets over multiple visits or observations, enabling the quantification of performance based on the specific parameters. This tool holds significance in delineating the technical specifications for future multi-object spectroscopy instrumentation. This will inform the development of new technologies for the next generation of telescopes using novel instrumentation techniques or the extension of existing technologies.
item.dc:creator: Ummee Tania Ahmed (Australian Astronomical Optics, Macquarie University, 105 Delhi Rd, North Ryde, NSW 2113, Australia), Andrew Hopkins (School of Mathematical and Physical Sciences, 12 Wallys Walk, Macquarie University, NSW 2109, Australia), Simon Ellis (Australian Astronomical Optics, Macquarie University, 105 Delhi Rd, North Ryde, NSW 2113, Australia)

item.title: Feasibility of Capillary-Driven Orbital Liquid Mirror Telescopes
item.description: arXiv:2608.31042v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Space-based liquid mirror telescopes (LMTs) have been recently proposed to overcome the scaling limits of traditional rigid mirrors. In these new space architectures, capillary forces would shape a reflective liquid into a spherical optical surface in microgravity. However, the equilibrium, stability, and dynamic behavior of such liquid interfaces remain largely uncharacterized under orbital perturbations. This study investigates the feasibility of space LMTs by combining axisymmetric capillary with thin-film models. Solar radiation pressure and self-gravitation are found to be the dominant perturbations in Sun--Earth L2 orbits, causing equilibrium deformations that exceed the $\lambda/20$ optical threshold at apertures above 0.86~m for visible ($\lambda = 380$~nm) and 1.58~m for near-infrared observatories ($\lambda = 2.5~\mu \mathrm{m}$). Micrometeoroid impacts self-heal within seconds to minutes, settling after filling requires years to decades at large apertures, and propulsive maneuvers breach optical limits within seconds to hours. These results highlight the need for interface control in large-scale systems such as NASA's 50~m Fluidic Telescope (FLUTE). Thermocapillary actuation supports apertures of 2.3/8.0~m (VIS/NIR) at $100~\mu \mathrm{K}$ and 10.6/37.7~m at $10~\mu \mathrm{K}$ resolution. Simultaneously, parasitic Marangoni flows impose sub-mK uniformity requirements for NIR and 1--$100~\mu \mathrm{K}$ for visible operation on any capillary LMT. Departing the capillary regime by imposing a surface-normal settling acceleration, ranging from 39~mm\,s$^{-2}$ (NIR,5~m) to 17~m\,s$^{-2}$ (VIS,50~m), is the most promising route to tens of meters in aperture. This approach enables a passive implementation, effectively suppressing perturbation induced interface distortions and thermal Marangoni flows. Keywords: Liquid mirror telescope, Optics, Space
item.dc:creator: Janoah Dietrich, \'Alvaro Romero-Calvo

item.title: EPIMETHEUS: Effective point spread function inferred from mosaics
item.description: arXiv:2609.26879v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate knowledge of the point spread function (PSF) is essential for a wide range of astronomical applications, from astrometry to precision photometry. However, deriving a robust average effective PSF (ePSF) from astronomical mosaics is particularly challenging due to the superposition of exposures taken at different epochs, under different observing conditions, and with varying position angles (PAs). To address this issue, we present EPIMETHEUS, an open-source Python library designed to manage the entire ePSF construction workflow, from initial star selection to final model generation. Built with a modular architecture, EPIMETHEUS avoids black-box methodologies, ensuring full transparency and giving the user complete control over the stellar sample to use for the ePSF building to meet specific scientific requirements. The software can process multiple images or mosaics simultaneously to retrieve the ePSF, a crucial feature when individual fields lack a sufficient number of bright, unsaturated stars. Candidate stars can be automatically filtered based on orientation and light concentration, with options for manually excluding stars through a semi-automatic visual inspection. Although EPIMETHEUS is specifically optimised to handle the roto-translation complexities inherent to multi-epoch mosaics, it is versatile and can be equally applied to derive ePSFs from simpler, single-orientation images where rotational corrections are not required. Finally, to demonstrate the software's capabilities and provide an immediate resource, we release empirical ePSFs for standard HST and JWST filters across the COSMOS, UDS, Abell 2744, and GOODS-S fields.
item.dc:creator: Pietro Benotto, Benedetta Vulcani, Vittoria Altomonte

item.title: Model-Based Retrieval of Four Years of JWST/NIRCam Wavefronts
item.description: arXiv:2610.40187v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The fidelity of data recovered by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) depends on precise monitoring of the mirror segments' surfaces and alignment. To this end, every few days the observatory takes pairs of defocused images of a reference star with its NIRCam instrument; a closed-source phase retrieval package is then employed to infer the wavefront. We here present camino (Computational Aberration Modelling and Inference for NIRCam Observations), an open-source algorithm to model NIRCam built in JAX using the differentiable Fresnel optics code dLUX and regularised maximum likelihood inference that has been conditioned on the entire archive of NIRCam wavefront sensing data. We typically improve the reduced chi-squared in fits to the defocused data from 60-65 to 12-13. We reconstruct the wavefront history of JWST from the beginning of science operations to early 2026. This open source implementation operates in parallel to the current STScI phase retrieval algorithm, allowing access by the broader scientific community to high-accuracy wavefront estimation and enabling its direct integration into science-analysis workflows. This represents a major step towards the ultimate goal of predictive calibration methods based on physics-based forward modelling, obviating the need for time-consuming observation of contemporaneous dedicated reference stars.
item.dc:creator: Shrishmoy Ray, Benjamin Pope, Louis Desdoigts, Hayden Greer, Milo Langker, Peter Tuthill, Marshall Perrin, Anand Sivaramakrishnan, Alexandra Greenbaum, Laurent Pueyo, Max Charles

item.title: Differential velocity cumulative distribution (DVCD): an efficient statistical method for binary-star analysis in large stellar catalogues using radial velocities
item.description: arXiv:2502.18577v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Binary stars are fundamental to astrophysics, providing critical insights into stellar evolution, galactic dynamics, and fundamental physics. However, the high dimensionality of orbital parameters and observational constraints present significant challenges in statistically characterizing their properties. In this study, we propose and implement a novel algorithm, the Differential Velocity Cumulative Distribution (DVCD), to analyze binary star systems using radial velocity data. The DVCD method demonstrates superior accuracy and computational efficiency compared to existing approaches, reducing computation time by factors of $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-5}$ under comparable conditions. We applied the DVCD algorithm to red giant samples from APOGEE DR16, dividing the dataset into 16 subsets based on $\log g$ and M/H. Our findings reveal that the binary fraction decreases with decreasing surface gravity and increasing metallicity, offering valuable constraints on the evolutionary processes of binary stars. This study underscores the potential of the DVCD method for large-scale statistical analyzes of binary systems.
item.dc:creator: Luo Feng, Zhao YongHeng, Liu Chao

item.title: Wide Area VISTA Extragalactic Survey (WAVES): Redshift-limited selection of targets for the Wide survey using decision-tree classification
item.description: arXiv:2510.11132v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Wide-Area VISTA Extragalactic Survey (WAVES) on the 4-metre Multi-Object Spectroscopic Telescope (4MOST) includes two flux-limited subsurveys with very high (95%) completeness requirements: Wide over $\sim\!1200$ deg$^2$ and Deep over $\sim\!65$ deg$^2$. Both are $Z$-band selected, and additionally redshift-limited, while the true redshifts are not known a priori but will only be measured by 4MOST. Here, we present a classification-based method to select the targets for WAVES-Wide. Rather than estimating individual redshifts for the input photometric galaxies, we assign probabilities of them being below $z=0.2$, the redshift limit of the subsurvey.This is done with the supervised machine learning approach of eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), trained and tested on a comprehensive spectroscopic sample overlapping with WAVES fields and using nine-band VST+VISTA photometry for the feature space. We check the performance of our classifier both for the fiducial WAVES-Wide limits, as well as for a range of neighboring redshift and magnitude thresholds, finding purity and completeness at the level of 90-95% depending on the test set. The metrics deteriorate for sources close to the selection limits and for test sets selected from DESI, not used in training. We apply the classifier trained on the full spectroscopic sample to the 8.6 million galaxies from the WAVES photometric catalog. This gives us about 1.2 million target candidates, reducing to 1 million if we apply an XGB probability threshold $P_\mathrm{XGB}(z\leq0.2) > 0.72$. Our work demonstrates that a machine-learning classifier could be used to select a flux- and redshift-limited sample from deep photometric data.
item.dc:creator: G. Kaur, M. Bilicki, S. Bellstedt, E. Tempel, W. A. Hellwing, I. Baldry, B. Bandi, S. Barsanti, S. Driver, N. Guerra-Varas, B. Holwerda, C. Lagos, J. Loveday, A. Robotham

item.title: Entropy-based classification of core-collapse supernova gravitational waves for nuclear equation-of-state inference
item.description: arXiv:2511.08010v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gravitational waves from core-collapse supernovae provide a unique probe of the physical processes occurring during stellar collapse and of the properties of dense nuclear matter. In this work we investigate the classification of supernova gravitational-wave signals associated with different nuclear equations of state using an entropy-based machine learning framework. The analysis combines signal decomposition, feature extraction, and feature selection techniques to identify informative characteristics of the waveforms and distinguish between different equation of state models. We evaluate the performance of several machine learning classifiers using a compact set of selected features and assess their robustness in the presence of detector noise. We find that entropy-based representations capture the underlying differences between waveform classes and enable accurate classification while maintaining better performance compared to raw data under noisy conditions. These results demonstrate the potential of complexity-based feature extraction as an efficient and interpretable approach for gravitational wave studies of core-collapse supernovae.
item.dc:creator: Aknur Sakan, Nurzhan Ussipov, Y. Sultan Abylkairov, Marat Zaidyn, Alisher Zhunuskanov, Almat Akhmetali, Jos\'e A. Font, Matthew C. Edwards, Ernazar Abdikamalov

item.title: Gaussian perturbation interpretability for regression techniques to understand retrieval black-boxes
item.description: arXiv:2601.21685v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Characterizing the atmospheres of large numbers of exoplanets from their observed spectra can answer key questions about planetary populations. Traditional retrievals are resource-intensive; machine-learning methods offer a fast alternative, but their complexity renders them black-boxes. Understanding how they reach their predictions allows us to inspect them for biases and verify predictions are based on physically plausible spectral features. Commonly used perturbation-based methods for explaining machine learning struggle with the strong correlations between inputs in spectra. We introduce Gaussian perturbation methodology for explaining black-box regression models with one-dimensional structured inputs, which addresses these issues by leveraging physical knowledge of spectral correlation. We compare it with naive perturbation of one wavelength bin at a time. Although traditional retrievals are built on physical forward models, their mapping from spectrum to retrieved parameters is a black-box. We therefore first demonstrate this methodology using TauREx-III as a proxy black-box retrieval on HST observations of HD 209458 b and JWST observations of HAT-P-26 b, showing the efficacy of Gaussian perturbation-based interpretability against a well-established, physically motivated retrieval framework, before applying it to a convolutional neural network retrieval of HAT-P-26 b. For the gases the retrievals constrain, the importance from Gaussian perturbation agrees with the expected importance, including at the core of the $CO_2$ band of HAT-P-26 b, where a degeneracy inverts the response. The method shows which parts of a spectrum a retrieval relies on, which the physics of its forward model alone does not, and shows the neural network has learned the same degeneracy.
item.dc:creator: Jools D. Clarke, Kai Hou Yip, Nikolaos Nikolaou

item.title: Assessing the robustness of amortized simulation-based inference to transient noise in gravitational-wave ringdowns
item.description: arXiv:2603.12032v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gravitational waves (GW) emitted by binary systems allow us to perform precision tests of general relativity in the strong field regime. Ringdown signals allow for probing black hole mass and spin with high precision in GW astronomy. With improvements in current and next-generation GW detectors, developing likelihood-free parameter inference methods is crucial. This is especially important when facing challenges such as non-standard noise, partial data, or incomplete signal models that prevent the use of analytical likelihood functions. In this work, we propose an amortized simulation-based inference strategy to estimate ringdown parameters directly. Specifically, our method is based on amortized neural posterior estimation, which trains a neural density estimator of the posterior for all data segments within the prior range. The results show that our trained amortized network achieves valid confidence coverage and yields posteriors in agreement with established Markov-chain methods at moderate signal-to-noise ratios. At higher signal-to-noise ratios, the recovered posteriors agree with the Markov-chain results in location, although the amplitude posterior is broader. The network provides inference speeds that are orders of magnitude faster. Furthermore, we evaluate the robustness of the method against transient noise contamination. Our results indicate that the timing of glitch injection significantly affects estimation bias, in particular when the glitch contaminates the early, high-amplitude portion of the signal. This study not only provides an efficient and statistically validated inference framework under the tested conditions for ringdown analysis but also lays a foundation for developing robust data-processing pipelines for future GW astronomy in realistic noise environments.
item.dc:creator: Song-Tao Liu, Tian-Yang Sun, Yu-Xin Wang, Yong-Xin Zhang, Shang-Jie Jin, Jing-Fei Zhang, Xin Zhang

item.title: The Quantum Noise Fraction and the addressable fraction in High-Frequency Gravitational Wave Detection
item.description: arXiv:2605.00053v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The quantum noise fraction $\beta$, the share of a detector's noise power that is quantum in origin, sets a ceiling $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{max}} = 1/\sqrt{1-\beta}$ on the sensitivity improvement that removing quantum-origin noise can yield. In the kHz--GHz band the readout degree of freedom is a bosonic mode and $\beta = 1/(2\bar{n}_{\mathrm{th}}+1)$, with $\bar{n}_{\mathrm{th}}$ the Bose--Einstein occupation. Quantum noise then dominates only on the cold side of the thermal frontier $k_BT\ln 3 = \hbar\omega$ (above 229 MHz at 10 mK), which governs mechanical resonators and electromagnetic cavities alike; a real readout turns it into a joint condition on the occupation and on the excess noise of the readout chain. On a multimode acoustic antenna the frontier can be observed within one device, since the logarithmic slope of $\sqrt{S_hQ}$ along the odd-overtone comb increases by one half across it whatever the dependence of the quality factor on overtone number. On this antenna, crossing the frontier costs more in classical sensitivity than quantum enhancement returns. For a GHz mode of an existing bulk acoustic wave device at 10 mK, $\beta = 0.984$ and $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{max}} = 7.8$. That ceiling cannot be reached with a linear readout, because with intrinsic damping the zero-point term is the force noise of the bath, fixed by the fluctuation--dissipation theorem. The addressable fraction $\beta_a$ excludes it: at the standard quantum limit the same mode has $\beta = 0.992$ but $\beta_a = 0.496$, an available improvement of 1.41 against a ceiling of 11.0. An array of $10^4$ such devices cross-correlated for one year reaches $3.6\times 10^{-24}$ Hz$^{-1/2}$ for an integration bandwidth equal to the linewidth; even granting $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{max}} = 7.8$ in full, a factor $1.0\times 10^{10}$ above the big-bang-nucleosynthesis bound remains, and it is classical.
item.dc:creator: Sergio Gaudio

item.title: A New Global Chemical Equilibrium Code: Refractory Element Signatures in Super-Earths and Sub-Neptunes
item.description: arXiv:2605.07833v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The atmospheres of super-Earths and sub-Neptunes can be strongly modified by chemical exchange with their molten interiors during long-lived magma ocean phases. Interpreting atmospheric observations requires fast models that self-consistently couple atmospheric chemistry to the composition of the planetary interior. We present an updated, CPU-based implementation of the global chemical equilibrium (GCE) framework from H. E. Schlichting & E. D. Young (2022), which computes the equilibrium composition of a coupled metal-silicate-gas system. The numerical solver has been improved using a gradient-based optimizer, reducing the computational cost of solving the chemical network by more than two orders of magnitude and enabling large parameter studies. We apply the framework to a large synthetic population of planets and explore the imprint of bulk refractory composition of Mg, Si, and Fe on atmospheric properties in the end member case that hydrogen dissolution increases unbound with pressure. We consider planets with different masses, thermal states, and volatile inventories. We find that the atmospheric mass fraction and atmospheric metal mass fraction are primarily controlled by the temperature at the atmosphere-magma ocean interface and the planetary water budget, while the accreted hydrogen mass fraction plays a minor role because most hydrogen dissolves into the interior. For planets that accreted water, the refractory ratios Mg/Si and Fe/Si strongly influence carbon partitioning between the gas, silicate, and metal phases, producing large variations in atmospheric metal mass fraction and C/O ratios. These results demonstrate that atmospheric compositions of sub-Neptunes depend sensitively on both the volatile inventory and the bulk composition of rocky material, providing new constraints for interpreting atmospheric observations. The new GCE code is open-source.

item.title: SPLIT: Loosely-coherent inference of long-inspiral gravitational-wave sources for robustness against modeling and data outliers
item.description: arXiv:2606.13728v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect gravitational waves (GWs) from dozens of extreme- and intermediate-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs/IMRIs). These sources will stay in-band for months to years, offering extraordinary scientific potential. However, their fully phase-coherent analysis standard in current pipelines imposes stringent waveform accuracy requirements; failing to model the signal over such long durations can result in significant systematic biases. To address this, we formulate a robust Bayesian inference framework that segments the data into blocks, infers each block coherently, and recombines the results using loosely-coherent phase information. By restricting full phase-tracking to much shorter block durations, this approach prevents significant accumulation of phase errors. We implement this methodology in \textsc{SPLIT} (Segmented Posteriors for Long-Inspiral Templates), a GPU-accelerated Python package. Applying \textsc{SPLIT} to an environment-rich injection, we demonstrate that while a fully-coherent vacuum-GR analysis incurs a maximum 1D systematic bias of $\approx 4.8\sigma$ from the truth, the shorter integration window of our loosely-coherent approach restricts such biases to $\lesssim 0.5\sigma$. Overall, despite a fractional loss of optimal signal-to-noise ratio, the substantial improvement in parameter accuracy offered by our method presents a highly advantageous trade-off for LISA and other future GW detectors.
item.dc:creator: Shubham Kejriwal

item.title: Correcting stellar contamination in transmission spectroscopy with contemporaneous monitoring: Application to GJ 1214 b
item.description: arXiv:2609.35721v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transmission spectroscopy is an essential tool for characterising the atmospheres of transiting exoplanets. However, stellar surface inhomogeneities contaminate transmission spectra, posing a major challenge to high-precision observations such as those from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). We develop and apply methods to correct for stellar contamination, improving the accuracy of exoplanet atmospheric characterisation. We obtained coordinated multi-band photometry and high-resolution spectroscopy around JWST observations of GJ 1214 b and applied two frameworks: (i) a StarSim inversion, which infers stellar activity parameters from the monitoring data and propagates them to corrections; and (ii) UnSPOTTER, in which neural networks trained on StarSim simulations learn the mapping from monitoring data to corrections. Both frameworks agree within uncertainties and indicate that the JWST observations of GJ 1214 occurred at a favourable rotation phase with low stellar contamination. For UnSPOTTER, the inferred corrections can be constrained at approximately 10-30 ppm across the JWST wavelength range, implying post-correction residuals of the same order. If the same system were observed near activity maximum, the predicted contamination would be strongly chromatic and affect atmospheric retrievals, highlighting the importance of coordinated monitoring and robust activity correction techniques. The two approaches are complementary but serve different roles. The inversion yields physically interpretable parameters and surface maps, whereas UnSPOTTER marginalises over surface-configuration degeneracies and provides tighter predictive corrections within its validated simulation domain. Our pipeline can potentially be generalised to other active stars: with multi-band and multi-technique monitoring around JWST visits, it can provide activity forecasts for scheduling and activity corrections.
